video_title: Does America Deserve to Win the AI Race? Erik Voorhees Says No: Uneasy Money
gist: Venice founder/CEO Erik Voorhees tells Unchained's Uneasy Money hosts (Kane, Taylor Monahan) that frontier AI labs emerged from a top-down, government-cooperative academic culture fundamentally opposed to crypto's decentralization ethos, and that Venice is built as an uncensored AI aggregator funded by equity (not token sales) with its VVV token engineered to go deflationary via revenue-funded buybacks. He argues inference economics are collapsing toward zero margin (DeepSeek roughly 50x cheaper than Claude Max-equivalent throughput; Anthropic losing money on $200/month plans) and that local/edge model hosting is a bad financial trade that will never out-compete data-center scale. He says he would back Chinese AI models over American ones if they better preserve individual privacy and freedom, rejecting nationalist 'America must win' framing amid talk of roughly 30% government stakes in AI labs.

insights.claim: Stripe's acquisition of OpenRouter — a roughly two-year-old API marketplace matching inference providers with consumers — is one of the most successful examples of a crypto-adjacent team fully pivoting into AI infrastructure, having exited crypto/NFT origins entirely to build pure AI inference brokerage.
insights.speaker: Kane (host)
insights.so_what: Signals AI-inference marketplaces are now attractive enough M&A targets for major fintech acquirers, and that a 'full pivot' out of crypto into AI infra can be a faster path to an exit than staying crypto-native.

insights.claim: Hermes, a formerly crypto-native project, fully pivoted out of crypto into AI about two and a half years ago, illustrating a broader pattern of crypto teams abandoning crypto entirely for AI rather than combining the two.
insights.speaker: Kane (host)
insights.so_what: Useful comparator for evaluating whether a crypto-AI hybrid (like Venice) or a full pivot (like OpenRouter, Hermes) captures more value as AI inference demand grows.

insights.claim: Erik Voorhees positions Venice as the leading example of a genuine crypto-plus-AI hybrid — incorporating crypto primitives (a token, incentive mechanisms) directly into an AI product rather than abandoning crypto for AI like OpenRouter or Hermes did.
insights.speaker: Erik Voorhees (guest, Venice CEO)
insights.so_what: Frames Venice's differentiated bet: that crypto incentive design (not just payments) is the value-add crypto brings to AI, rather than crypto being obsolete once AI arrives.

insights.claim: Because nearly all major AI labs are private (Google being the exception), ordinary people cannot get equity exposure to AI's wealth creation even as they fear AI taking their jobs; Voorhees says Venice's VVV token is meant to give everyday users a stake in an AI company's growth from its earliest days.
insights.speaker: Erik Voorhees (guest, Venice CEO)
insights.so_what: Positions token-based AI companies as a structural workaround to retail investors being locked out of private frontier-AI equity — a differentiated access thesis for crypto-AI hybrids.
insights.quote: the all the major AI labs are private, you know, with the exception of Google

insights.claim: Venice is planning (not yet announced or deployed) a mechanism that takes a portion of a user's subscription or credit spend, uses it to buy VVV tokens, and returns those tokens to the user contingent on continued platform use — turning paying customers into token holders via loyalty rather than a direct token sale.
insights.speaker: Erik Voorhees (guest, Venice CEO)
insights.so_what: A reusable playbook for AI/consumer apps to distribute token ownership without a marketed token sale, increasing retention ('stickiness') and creating organic buy pressure funded by product revenue.
insights.quote: if we can take some of what Venice is earning and give it back to them in the coin of the of the project

insights.claim: Voorhees argues a recurring failure mode in crypto is that tokens became self-referential 'the product' itself rather than serving an underlying purpose — contrasting with Bitcoin (serving as base money) and Ethereum (ETH powering a smart-contract platform), which each have a distinct product the token supports.
insights.speaker: Erik Voorhees (guest, Venice CEO)
insights.so_what: A screening heuristic for investors: discount tokens that lack a clear non-token product/purpose, since self-referential coin-as-product designs tend toward speculative races to the bottom.
insights.quote: Bitcoin is serving the purpose and the good of of base money

insights.claim: Voorhees argues regulatory risk perversely pushed crypto builders toward meaningless memecoins rather than utility tokens after the ICO boom and DeFi summer, because a token attached to real utility had a higher chance of being deemed a security by regulators than a token with no stated purpose.
insights.speaker: Erik Voorhees (guest, Venice CEO)
insights.so_what: Explains the multi-year memecoin dominance as a rational response to securities-law incentives, implying regulatory clarity (not just market cycles) is a prerequisite for utility-token projects to compete again.
insights.quote: if you had a project that that had utility to it and you had a token, it had a higher chance of being deemed a security than if you just released a memecoin

themes.theme: Tokens vs Equity: Venice's Capital Structure

insights.claim: In its recent raise, Venice chose to sell equity rather than tokens because the team does not want to sell VVV at all; instead, the equity investors received warrants/options to buy VVV at a fixed price, vesting over four years, so they are incentivized toward Venice's unorthodox token-burn strategy.
insights.speaker: Erik Voorhees (guest, Venice CEO)
insights.so_what: A template capital-structure move for token-issuing startups raising VC money: sell the more VC-legible asset (equity) while retaining the scarcer/strategic asset (token), using warrants to keep investor and token-holder interests aligned.
insights.quote: So they can they have an option that they can buy token at a certain price um which then vests over four years.

insights.claim: Voorhees frames equity as the 'infinitely inflatable' asset that Venice will dilute freely, while VVV is designed to be structurally deflationary — the company intends to shrink total VVV supply over time via revenue-funded buybacks/burns, with no equivalent plan to shrink the equity supply.
insights.speaker: Erik Voorhees (guest, Venice CEO)
insights.so_what: A concrete dual-asset capital allocation strategy investors can monitor: rising equity dilution paired with falling token supply implies management is deliberately routing value preference toward token holders over time.
insights.quote: our our entire strategy with VBV is to take it deflationary. So the actual token supply will shrink with time.

insights.claim: Voorhees argues Venice's equity holders and token holders are not structurally misaligned because insiders (including himself, the largest equity holder) and the company itself hold both assets, and the company holds more VVV than anyone else — so tokens burned with revenue benefit equity value rather than harming it.
insights.speaker: Erik Voorhees (guest, Venice CEO)
insights.so_what: Rebuts the common assumption that token buybacks/burns are automatically dilutive or adversarial to equity holders in a dual-asset company — a nuance investors evaluating token+equity cap tables should check for.
insights.quote: I'm the biggest equity holder of all. Why would I why would I do that?

insights.claim: Kane recounts running a prior 'pure token' project with no legal entity at all (fully DAO-governed, all entities and foundation shut down) around 2019, which survived without SEC enforcement despite the team's own lawyers considering the structure legally insane.
insights.speaker: Kane (host)
insights.so_what: A real-world data point on regulatory risk tolerance for zero-entity, fully decentralized token projects — relevant precedent for founders weighing entity-free structures against the equity-plus-token model Venice chose instead.
insights.quote: the SEC just missed the memo on that one, but we literally had no protection.

insights.claim: Voorhees says Venice needs a legal entity because AI is capital-intensive (tens of millions of dollars spent on GPUs), not for regulatory protection — in his experience, having a corporate entity 'only invites regulatory scrutiny' rather than shielding the company from it.
insights.speaker: Erik Voorhees (guest, Venice CEO)
insights.so_what: Challenges the common founder assumption that incorporating protects against regulatory risk; investors should weight entity structure decisions as capital-raising necessities, not liability shields.
insights.quote: having an entity is only only invites regulatory scrutiny frankly.

themes.theme: AI Culture vs Crypto Culture: The Centralization Divide

insights.claim: Voorhees frames a cultural split: crypto emerged around shared principles of decentralization, privacy, and individual sovereignty, while frontier AI labs emerged from a decades-long academic tradition whose dominant philosophy holds that powerful technology should be tightly controlled by the right people at the top.
insights.speaker: Erik Voorhees (guest, Venice CEO)
insights.so_what: Explains why AI-lab governance defaults to centralized, government-cooperative models rather than crypto-style open protocols — a structural reason to expect AI-lab policy positions to keep favoring regulation and control.
insights.quote: very very top down um very centralization of power and make sure that the person in charge is the right person kind of mentality.

insights.claim: Voorhees says he half-jokingly founded Venice as an 'AI safety company' to prevent a dystopian outcome where machine intelligence becomes state-mediated through the official mouthpiece of centralized, government-cooperative AI labs.
insights.speaker: Erik Voorhees (guest, Venice CEO)
insights.so_what: Reframes 'AI safety' as decentralization/anti-censorship rather than content moderation — a distinct investment thesis segment (decentralized/uncensored AI infra) separate from mainstream AI-safety-branded companies.
insights.quote: I like to half joke that Venice was set up as a as an AI safety company basically prevent that kind of thing from happening.

insights.claim: The core divide in how crypto people versus AI-lab people respond to powerful, potentially dangerous technology comes down to a single framing choice: 'this is powerful and dangerous, so centralize it' versus 'this is powerful and dangerous, so decentralize it' — crypto people default to the latter, most AI-lab people to the former.
insights.speaker: Kane (host)
insights.so_what: A quick mental model for classifying any new AI/crypto governance proposal by which side of this framing its backers implicitly hold, useful for anticipating policy positioning of labs vs protocols.
insights.quote: this thing is obviously powerful and may be dangerous thus let's centralize it or this thing is powerful and may be dangerous thus let's decentralize it.

insights.claim: Voorhees claims none of the frontier AI labs are actually restraining their internal model capabilities — they only restrain what they publicly release — meaning released models likely understate how far ahead labs' internal frontier models actually are.
insights.speaker: Erik Voorhees (guest, Venice CEO)
insights.so_what: Implies public benchmark leaderboards and 'released' model capability materially understate true frontier lab capability, a gap investors should factor into competitive/regulatory forecasts.
insights.quote: My guess is that none of them are actually restraining themselves.

insights.claim: Open-source models are now trailing the frontier closed models by only about one to two months while running at roughly 10% of the cost, evidence that the capability gap between open and closed models is compressing fast even as absolute frontier capability keeps advancing.
insights.speaker: Erik Voorhees (guest, Venice CEO)
insights.so_what: Supports a thesis that closed-model moats are shrinking on a lag basis, pressuring the pricing power of frontier-lab API businesses and favoring aggregator/infra plays like Venice that are model-agnostic.
insights.quote: there's like these open source models that are now one or two months behind them and catching up uh at at 10% of the cost.

insights.claim: AI labs face a delicate political trade-off in Washington: arguing frontier models are dangerous in order to get competing Chinese models regulated can also invite regulation that ends up constraining their own models.
insights.speaker: co-host
insights.so_what: A risk to watch in AI-lab lobbying strategy: safety-framed calls for China-focused AI regulation could boomerang into domestic compliance costs or capability restrictions for the labs pushing them.
insights.quote: that can also mean that that their own company starts getting nerfed or caught up in the confines of it.

themes.theme: AI Geopolitics: US, China, and Nationalization Risk

insights.claim: Voorhees says he is not a nationalist and does not care about the US as a nation, only about principles like individual freedom and privacy — he explicitly states he would back Chinese AI models over American ones if the Chinese models better express those principles.
insights.speaker: Erik Voorhees (guest, Venice CEO)
insights.so_what: Reframes 'US vs China AI race' investment and policy debates around which jurisdiction's models actually preserve user privacy/freedom, rather than national origin — a lens for evaluating open-weight Chinese models on their own terms.
insights.quote: if uh if Chinese models better express those principles, then I care more about the Chinese models than I do about the American models.

insights.claim: Voorhees claims the multi-decade trend is that the US government is increasingly controlling and monitoring its own citizens while the Chinese government has become comparatively more market-oriented — a reversal of the conventional US-freedom-vs-China-authoritarianism narrative.
insights.speaker: Erik Voorhees (guest, Venice CEO)
insights.so_what: Challenges investors and policymakers to reassess jurisdictional-risk assumptions in AI/crypto regulation rather than defaulting to 'US = free market, China = authoritarian.'
insights.quote: the meta trend is that the that the US is controlling and monitoring its people increasingly and the Chinese government is actually doing less

insights.claim: The hosts and Voorhees note that proposals for the US government to take an equity stake (roughly 30% has been floated) in, or effectively nationalize, private AI labs have entered the mainstream policy conversation with surprisingly little pushback, despite resembling the state-directed industrial policy usually associated with China.
insights.speaker: Erik Voorhees (guest, Venice CEO)
insights.so_what: A live regulatory tail risk for AI-lab investors and employees: partial government ownership/control of frontier labs is being normalized in US discourse, which could reshape governance, IP, and export dynamics.
insights.quote: yeah like 30% nationalization of these labs is fine like

insights.claim: Voorhees says he has zero faith in the political process and does not vote for presidential candidates because state institutional momentum cannot be reformed; he sees permissionless technology like Bitcoin — which required no vote or anyone's permission to use — as the only real avenue for opting out of the system.
insights.speaker: Erik Voorhees (guest, Venice CEO)
insights.so_what: Explains his underlying investment philosophy for Venice and crypto generally: build technological exit options rather than pursue political reform, since he believes policy channels are structurally unresponsive.
insights.quote: I have zero faith in the political process. Like I I don't vote for presidential candidates.

insights.claim: Voorhees says decentralized AI inference is fairly workable today, but decentralized AI training is not yet competitive — some companies are making progress on decentralized training, but it remains an open, unresolved bottleneck ('TBD') for a fully decentralized AI stack.
insights.speaker: Erik Voorhees (guest, Venice CEO)
insights.so_what: Identifies decentralized training infrastructure as the current frontier gap for the crypto-AI decentralization thesis — a specific sub-sector to watch for investable breakthroughs.
insights.quote: inference can be done fairly well in a decentralized way.

themes.theme: Inference Economics: The Race to Zero Margin

insights.claim: Voorhees says Anthropic is losing money hand over fist on its roughly $200/month subscription plans because heavy users can consume the equivalent of $10,000 worth of API tokens for that flat fee, and the subsidy's sustainability depends on how large that loss center is relative to Anthropic's total revenue.
insights.speaker: Erik Voorhees (guest, Venice CEO)
insights.so_what: A red flag on the unit economics of flat-fee 'unlimited' AI subscription plans — investors should track whether Anthropic (and peers) can sustain or must reprice these heavily subsidized consumer tiers.
insights.quote: Anthropic is losing money handover fist on those plus $200 a month plans.

insights.claim: Kane cites DeepSeek's V4 Pro-era release as being roughly 50x cheaper than the equivalent token throughput available via a $200/month Claude Max plan, illustrating how volatile and fast-moving per-token inference pricing is across model releases.
insights.speaker: Kane (host)
insights.so_what: A concrete example that inference pricing can reprice by an order of magnitude within a single model-generation cycle, making inference cost forecasting and vendor lock-in decisions unusually risky.
insights.quote: Deepseek as an example, right, came out when when uh V4 Pro came out um and like was 50 times cheaper, right?

insights.claim: Voorhees argues the falling cost of AI intelligence is structurally good for civilization (comparable to falling food or electricity costs) but structurally bad for anyone selling raw inference/tokens, because commoditized, VC-subsidized competition is driving inference margins toward zero — 'no one's going to make any material money on selling tokens.'
insights.speaker: Erik Voorhees (guest, Venice CEO)
insights.so_what: Core investment implication: raw-inference-selling businesses are a structurally bad long-term bet regardless of near-term revenue growth; value capture must come from a layer above commodity tokens (UX, bundling, subscriptions).
insights.quote: the end state is that no one's going to make any material money on selling tokens,

insights.claim: Voorhees says the only company that has historically 'de-commoditized' a deflationary hardware/compute trend is Apple, which wraps commoditizing components in a branded software-and-hardware experience people pay a premium for, despite the underlying compute/storage costs collapsing.
insights.speaker: Erik Voorhees (guest, Venice CEO)
insights.so_what: A benchmark for evaluating whether any AI inference or infra company can escape commoditized-token economics — the Apple precedent suggests only deep UX/hardware-software integration, not raw model access, can sustain premium pricing.
insights.quote: The only people that have really pulled off the ability to like uncommonize themselves are Apple, right?

insights.claim: Venice's actual margin structure: API/premium-credit sales are treated as a 'race to zero' with no material expected profit, while its $18/month Pro subscription is the higher-margin product even though Venice loses roughly $6 to $10 per subscriber per month, because subscribers get broad model access without per-request billing friction.
insights.speaker: Erik Voorhees (guest, Venice CEO)
insights.so_what: Shows that in AI-inference businesses, subscription bundling (not metered API sales) is where usable margin currently exists — a concrete unit-economics data point for anyone modeling AI-infra business models.
insights.quote: someone's paying $18 a month and we spend or lose $6 to $10 a month on the person.

insights.claim: Voorhees says Venice deliberately does not offer Anthropic-style flat-fee unlimited plans on its API specifically, because APIs are mechanistic and their usage can be automated at scale, making heavily subsidized free/flat API tiers dangerous to abuse — unlike app-based plans, which have usage caps most users never hit.
insights.speaker: Erik Voorhees (guest, Venice CEO)
insights.so_what: A risk-management principle for any token/API business: subsidized flat-rate pricing is far riskier on programmatic (API) surfaces than on human-facing app surfaces, since automation can exploit the former at scale.
insights.quote: So it's very dangerous to give any kind of free thing over an API, right?

insights.claim: Kane says his team's monthly AI inference/API bills reached roughly $100,000 to $200,000, prompting internal confusion when an engineer found he could spend more tokens on a personal $200/month Claude Max plan than the metered API billing suggested was economical.
insights.speaker: Kane (host)
insights.so_what: Real-world evidence that flat-fee consumer AI plans can be economically irrational to bypass in favor of metered API billing for heavy users, reinforcing that subsidized subscription tiers are currently underpriced relative to API rates.
insights.quote: we had uh like 100 200k uh monthly bills for inference, right?

insights.claim: Voorhees argues running AI models locally on high-end personal hardware should never be framed as a way to save money — due to economies of scale in industrial GPU/server manufacturing, large-scale data centers will always be more cost-efficient than local inference, making the 'save money by going local' pitch a myth or illusion.
insights.speaker: Erik Voorhees (guest, Venice CEO)
insights.so_what: Investors and builders should not underwrite local/edge-inference hardware plays on a cost-savings thesis; the real value proposition is control, privacy, and hands-on learning, not economics.
insights.quote: the the point of of running things locally and never and should never be about saving money because you won't it's a it's a myth or an illusion.

insights.claim: Kane bought a $20,000 Mac Studio with 512GB of RAM to run local models and found the 'payback curve' was never good and has only gotten worse over time, because the machine cannot run enough inference volume to justify its cost versus simply paying for cloud/API inference.
insights.speaker: Kane (host)
insights.so_what: A concrete real-world data point confirming Voorhees's thesis: even well-resourced buyers of top-tier local-inference hardware are finding the economics worsening, not improving, as cloud inference costs keep falling.
insights.quote: the payback curve is going the wrong direction for me

insights.claim: Voorhees predicts the average person will likely never run frontier models locally at scale, because whatever compute someone can afford at the edge, a server can run something roughly 10x as intelligent for less — so the real contest is not local-vs-cloud but which servers people are permitted to access (state-licensed/approved data centers vs. sovereignty-preserving ones).
insights.speaker: Erik Voorhees (guest, Venice CEO)
insights.so_what: Reframes the decentralization battle in AI away from 'run it yourself' hardware plays and toward preserving open, unrestricted access to server-side inference — the more consequential policy and infrastructure fight to watch.
insights.quote: whatever you can run at the edge you can run something 10x as intelligent from a server.

themes.theme: Model Aggregation, Censorship Layers, and Trust at Venice

insights.claim: Voorhees argues AI model outputs are shaped by an often-invisible 'layer' of corporate policy committees (at labs like Anthropic and OpenAI) and state-regulator input sitting between the user and the raw model, which he calls opaque, deceptive, and easily abused since users can't see where its boundaries are or what it's changing.
insights.speaker: Erik Voorhees (guest, Venice CEO)
insights.so_what: A due-diligence lens for evaluating AI products: the gap between 'the model' and 'what you actually get' is a hidden, unaudited policy layer, which is a governance and trust risk distinct from the model's raw capability.
insights.quote: It's got this opaque undefined like MIDI layer, right?

insights.claim: Venice adds no content-moderation filter on top of model inputs or outputs, but the underlying models themselves carry varying built-in censorship from training, and 'uncensored' fine-tuned variants of a given model typically come with reduced intelligence — creating an ongoing UX trade-off Venice has to manage.
insights.speaker: Erik Voorhees (guest, Venice CEO)
insights.so_what: Highlights a real capability-vs-freedom trade-off in uncensored AI products that investors in this niche should underwrite: 'uncensored' access isn't free — it can cost measurable intelligence/quality.
insights.quote: typically the uncensored versions of the models decrease the um intelligence of the model.

insights.claim: For users who don't want to rely on Venice's reputation alone, Venice offers trusted-execution-environment (TEE) and end-to-end-encrypted model access where the entire inference round trip can be independently attested by an outside technical party, verifying the no-logging claim rather than requiring trust.
insights.speaker: Erik Voorhees (guest, Venice CEO)
insights.so_what: A concrete verifiability feature (cryptographic attestation) that differentiates privacy-focused AI infra from reputation-only 'trust us' privacy claims — a due-diligence checklist item for evaluating competing private-inference providers.
insights.quote: The entire round trip of the inference uh can be attested by an outsider who's mildly technical.

insights.claim: Venice operates as a model-agnostic aggregator across text, image, video, and audio rather than training its own models, integrating essentially every major closed- and open-source model behind one API/app; the team now gets new model releases live often within 30 minutes, up from roughly monthly releases when Venice started to multiple releases per day now.
insights.speaker: Erik Voorhees (guest, Venice CEO)
insights.so_what: Illustrates both the acceleration of model release cadence industry-wide (a leading indicator of AI competitive intensity) and the operational value of an aggregator layer that abstracts users away from tracking that churn themselves.
insights.quote: we we get models live often within 30 minutes of them being released.

insights.claim: Venice only labels a model 'private' (no data retention, nothing to subpoena) once it self-hosts the open-weight model under its own zero-data-retention infrastructure; models accessed via their original closed-source labs or third-party hosts (e.g., GLM via the Chinese host ZAI) are explicitly not marked private because Venice doesn't control or fully trust that third party's data handling.
insights.speaker: Erik Voorhees (guest, Venice CEO)
insights.so_what: A concrete, checkable trust framework for evaluating any AI privacy claim: 'private' should mean self-hosted with verifiable zero-retention, not merely 'accessible via an API,' since third-party hosting reintroduces a data-custody risk.
insights.quote: Venice doesn't trust any thirdparty company like that enough to list it as private.

insights.claim: Venice initially self-hosted inference on leased GPU hardware and found it was competent at running image models but that LLM serving was far more operationally complex (caching, configuration); it shifted to zero-data-retention infrastructure partners, then after its recent Series A began buying its own GPUs to build in-house LLM-serving competency.
insights.speaker: Erik Voorhees (guest, Venice CEO)
insights.so_what: Shows the real operational learning curve of standing up multi-modal AI infrastructure — image-model serving and LLM serving are materially different competencies, a useful benchmark for anyone building or evaluating AI infra teams.
insights.quote: we learned that we were actually quite good at running image models, but LLMs are for some reason much more complicated.

insights.claim: Voorhees frames a practical model-selection trade-off: a model that is 3-4% less intelligent but 3x cheaper to run can be called multiple times with self-validation/voting to match or exceed the output quality of a smarter, more expensive single-shot model, meaning raw benchmark intelligence isn't the only variable that should drive model choice.
insights.speaker: Erik Voorhees (guest, Venice CEO)
insights.so_what: A cost-optimization framework for teams building AI products: brute-forcing with a cheaper, slightly weaker model can beat paying a premium for marginally higher single-shot intelligence, changing how 'best model' should be evaluated for production use.
insights.quote: if you can have like a model that's three or 4% less intelligent, but you can run it three times for the same price.

insights.claim: Voorhees notes AI model outputs are inherently non-deterministic, so to sanity-check a model's real answer (e.g., when testing for censorship or consistency) he recommends asking the same question multiple times and merging the answers rather than trusting any single response as fully representative.
insights.speaker: Erik Voorhees (guest, Venice CEO)
insights.so_what: A practical due-diligence tactic for anyone auditing AI model behavior (censorship, factuality, consistency) — single-response testing can be misleading given model output variance.
insights.quote: you got to ask the same question three times and and merge the the answers.
